records.title: Hinkley Point C construction cost and the permissions still ahead
records.scope: The two-unit Hinkley Point C development in Somerset, United Kingdom, counted once as an integrated project. Hinkley Point A, Hinkley Point B and Sizewell C are outside this identity.
records.answer: Hinkley Point C is a construction project with a revised delivery baseline. EDF's February 2026 plan targets Unit 1 in 2030; recent fire-safety compliance does not authorize generation or demonstrate delivered electricity.
records.stage: Under construction; issuer schedule and later regulatory permissions remain distinct

identity_decision.rationale: One named two-unit development with an identified licensee and site. Neither reactor is counted again as a child project, and nearby older stations and Sizewell C contribute no identity to this dossier. It was absent from the retained 54-project inventory.

timeline.event: ONR granted the site licence for two EPR reactors.
EDF announced its final investment decision.
EDF published the revised cost and schedule baseline.
ONR reported MEH alliance fire-notice compliance, with trials continuing.

sections.heading: One project with staged regulatory permissions
sections.text: ONR identifies NNB Generation Company (HPC) Ltd as the licensee for the Somerset development. Its historical account records the 2012 site licence, the 2016 investment decision and consent for nuclear safety-related construction in March 2017. The licence creates duties and a regulatory framework; it does not make every later activity automatically permissible. ONR describes further permissions through construction, installation and commissioning. The useful unit of analysis is therefore the named plant and the activity being authorized, not the broad label approved nuclear project.

sections.heading: Cost figures need their price basis
sections.text: EDF's February 20 presentation puts completion cost at £35 billion in 2015 sterling, excluding interim interest. It targets Unit 1 operation in 2030 and Unit 2 commissioning twelve months later. A further twelve-month delay would move Unit 1 to 2031 and add about £1 billion on the same price basis. Those figures are a dated management baseline, not an observed final bill. Mixing them with nominal spending, financing costs or a different year's currency value would create a misleading comparison.

sections.heading: Concrete progress does not measure the whole plant
sections.text: The same presentation reports Unit 1 civil works at 94 percent by concrete volume at the end of 2025, while the mechanical, electrical and heating programme remained behind schedule. These are different denominators. The concrete measure says something useful about one package of work, but cannot be applied to testing, integration or readiness to supply electricity. For readers comparing large projects, the central question is which unfinished systems control the next transition, rather than which percentage appears largest in a progress announcement.

sections.heading: Safety improvement has a defined scope
sections.text: On November 16, ONR reported that five MEH alliance organisations had complied with fire enforcement notices. It also said further trials were continuing under regulatory monitoring. This is a meaningful improvement in a specific construction-safety account. It should neither disappear behind a general delay narrative nor become a claim that all site obligations are closed. A compliance result answers the requirements of the notices concerned; commissioning permissions and nuclear operating performance require their own records.

sections.heading: The local delivery system matters
sections.text: Somerset Council monitors Development Consent Order requirements and Section 106 obligations, including transport and socio-economic arrangements. That makes workforce access and accommodation part of the surrounding delivery system, even though they are not reactor components. The linked Somerset account examines housing separately. A sound comparison should keep construction employment, local residence, training activity and lasting household benefit distinct: each describes a different population and period. Spending inside a region is not, by itself, a measure of who gains or who bears additional costs.

sections.heading: What would change the delivery account
sections.text: The next decisive records are dated package-completion and commissioning permissions that identify the systems covered. After generation begins, unit-level output, outage duration and operating costs would support a different kind of assessment. The editorial test is a chain from authorized activity to completed equipment to repeated service, with forecasts preserved beside actual dates. Neither a successful safety correction nor another project's experience should fill a missing step in that chain.

next_artifacts: A later issuer schedule and cost baseline retaining price year and financing scope.
Named commissioning permissions and completed system tests, assessed independently of construction progress.
Actual unit-level operating output and outages after generation begins, alongside local service outcomes.

records.title: Olkiluoto 3 operating performance and the November outage return
records.scope: TVO's Olkiluoto 3 generating unit in Eurajoki, Finland. Olkiluoto 1, Olkiluoto 2 and Posiva's disposal facility are separate assets and are not counted or assigned this unit's outcomes.
records.answer: TVO reports that Olkiluoto 3 reconnected to the grid on November 17 after a 68-day outage. That is an operating event, but not proof of sustained full output or closure of the outage's regulatory follow-up.
records.stage: Operating unit; dated post-outage reconnection reported by the operator

identity_decision.rationale: One physically identified generating unit, absent from the retained eligible-project inventory. The whole Olkiluoto site is not counted as a parent in addition, and neither the other reactors nor Posiva's waste facility inherit OL3 generation or licensing evidence.

timeline.event: STUK issued a favourable safety statement before the government decision.
TVO announced the government operating licence through 2038.
TVO reported reconnection at 17:16, after 68 days.

sections.heading: Licensing and operation are different milestones
sections.text: STUK's February 2019 statement supported granting an operating licence but explicitly left the decision to the Finnish Government. TVO then announced the March 7 licence, valid through the end of 2038. Both accounts still distinguished a separate fuel-loading permission. This chronology matters because a licence date is not a generation-start date. It also identifies the operator responsible for safety. The present dossier follows OL3 itself, rather than treating every development at the Olkiluoto site as part of one undifferentiated operating asset.

sections.heading: Continuous production was not continuous full power
sections.text: TVO's October 23 announcement says OL3 generated throughout its eighteen-month operating cycle. It also describes two primary-coolant-pump faults that reduced output to approximately 1,300 MW, around 84 percent of full capacity, before the September outage. These statements are compatible: remaining connected and generating is different from delivering full rated power. The announcement's 18,113 GWh total covers all three Olkiluoto units during January to September, so it cannot be used as OL3's own production figure or as the numerator of a unit-level capacity factor.

sections.heading: The actual return supersedes the earlier forecast
sections.text: The October announcement forecast a November 7 return. TVO's later release reports reconnection on November 17 at 17:16 after 68 days out of service. It attributes the extended outage to inspection findings and additional repairs, including valve wear, and reports repairs to pump faults that had affected output. The approximately 80-hour ramp to full power remained a forecast in that release. Calendar time passing after publication cannot substitute for an observed output series confirming that the ramp was completed.

sections.heading: Outage findings need their own follow-up
sections.text: TVO also reports deviations involving shutdown, system testing and maintenance work, with reports prepared or being prepared for STUK. The operator says it is investigating causes and improvement measures. That admission belongs alongside the successful reconnection: returning to service and completing corrective-action review are different outcomes. A reader should be able to follow the event, the corrective action and any regulator disposition without assuming that a favourable operational announcement resolves the entire safety account.

sections.heading: Lifecycle dependencies extend beyond electricity
sections.text: STUK's 2019 assessment includes fuel and waste management and identifies Posiva's final-disposal project in the spent-fuel plan. That dependency is important, but it is not an identity merger. A disposal facility's safety assessment, its operating authorization and its actual service each need their own dates and scope. The same principle applies to comparisons between nuclear plants: technology in common does not transfer a particular site's licence, waste arrangement or demonstrated reliability to another project.

sections.heading: A useful reliability account needs comparable periods
sections.text: The next analytical step is a unit-specific series that identifies generation, available capacity, planned outages and unplanned reductions over consistent intervals. It should state how ramping and market-related reductions are treated before interpreting a percentage as equipment reliability. Corrective-action records should remain linked but separately assessed. This editorial test permits both progress and adverse findings to remain visible, rather than reducing the plant to either a first-power success story or a delay headline.

next_artifacts: Observed OL3 output after November 17 with interval, units and measurement basis.
A dated operator or STUK disposition on the identified outage deviations and corrective actions.
Comparable unit-level annual generation, availability and outage measures, excluding OL1 and OL2 totals.

records.title: Somerset housing and local services during Hinkley construction
records.scope: The Somerset Council unitary-authority area in England, statistical geography E06000066. This is not the wider ceremonial county, North Somerset or Bath and North East Somerset; individual towns are not additional place identities in this batch.
records.answer: Somerset's construction workforce and housing system operate on different timescales. Council evidence identifies immediate rental pressure alongside longer-term housing plans; neither planned homes nor project spending demonstrates relief for current households.
records.stage: Dated local housing and governance account; project-attributed net outcomes not established

identity_decision.rationale: One exact unitary-authority area, absent from the retained 25-place inventory. The administrative geography supports local-service analysis without treating the wider ceremonial county or every workforce destination as the same place. Hinkley remains a separate project identity.

timeline.event: Planning Data records the start of Somerset Council as the unitary authority.
The housing needs assessment evaluates construction pressure against a 2045 planning horizon.
Reference date for 13,149 registered Homefinder households, reported in September.

sections.heading: Define the place before comparing its outcomes
sections.text: Planning Data identifies Somerset Council as a unitary authority, with a start date of April 1, 2023 and statistical geography E06000066. That identifier gives this account a stable administrative scope. Historical district evidence still needs its original geography attached; it cannot automatically become a county-wide trend. Nor should the everyday name Somerset silently include neighbouring authorities. The place dossier follows housing and public responsibilities within this defined area, while recognising that workers and supply chains can cross its boundary.

sections.heading: Construction demand and long-term need differ
sections.text: The council-commissioned housing assessment, dated April 2026, discusses high pressure on smaller private rentals and lower-income households during Hinkley construction. It cites about 12,000 site workers in July 2025, rather than the original 5,600-worker planning assumption. Its conclusion that the construction effect does not add housing need across the full period to 2045 is a long-horizon planning judgment. It does not mean the intervening rental pressure has disappeared, or that every worker requires a separate dwelling.

sections.heading: The register describes households not a project impact
sections.text: The council's September housing announcement reports 13,149 households on Homefinder Somerset as of June 30, 2026. The total includes active applicants and households being considered for a property. It is therefore not a count of homeless people, unoccupied homes or households displaced by Hinkley. The council identifies several pressures, including affordability, population ageing and changing household size. Those distinctions prevent a general housing problem from being assigned wholly to one construction project without a causal study.

sections.heading: Local monitoring connects transport and accommodation
sections.text: Somerset Council describes a compliance role for Development Consent Order requirements and Section 106 obligations. Its transport group reviews workforce travel and traffic-management reports, while the socio-economic group follows accommodation, tourism, health and other indicators. These arrangements provide places to look for a local account, not proof that a transport or housing target has been met. A service claim needs the dated measure, its geographic coverage and the relevant threshold, followed by an actual decision where compliance is asserted.

sections.heading: Temporary solutions and permanent homes need separate tests
sections.text: The housing assessment discusses a proposed temporary campus near M5 Junction 24 using earlier proposal language. That does not establish a current planning disposition. Separately, the September council statement describes a strategy for 580 council homes over five years. These are different forms of supply, serving different populations and durations. Neither a campus proposal nor a housing programme target is an occupied home. The practical follow-up is the named application or funded scheme, then completion, availability and the households actually accommodated.

sections.heading: Measure who benefits and who remains under pressure
sections.text: A useful local series would track rents, vacancies, household placements and transport performance with consistent boundaries and periods. It would separate construction workers from established residents and distinguish temporary capacity from lasting housing stock. Public expenditure and resident experience would help explain distribution, not merely totals. These are editorial measurement priorities: the account does not infer that all housing pressure comes from Hinkley, that every planned home will be delivered, or that a regional economic benefit necessarily reaches the households facing the tightest market.

next_artifacts: Exact temporary-campus application and disposition, followed separately by delivered and occupied capacity.
Dated local rent, vacancy, placement and worker-residence measures on consistent geographic boundaries.
Funded housing and transport schemes with completion and service results rather than programme targets alone.
